mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__drou.mechanism: In a national census of post-tsunami mangrove planting sites in Sri Lanka, seedlings and propagules planted in the higher intertidal zone of the dry and arid zones suffered from drought and high irradiance [ev_establishment_survival_kodikara17_2].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__drou.conditionality: This is a single observational source; it describes stress at poorly sited plantings rather than measuring how much drought reduced survival, and it points to planting position along the tidal gradient as the controlling factor.

mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__extr.mechanism: Compilers judge mangrove regeneration in Senegal as coping well with local rainstorms and mangrove afforestation in Bangladesh as coping well with local thunderstorms [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1442_2011_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_4300_2019_local_thunderstorm].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__extr.conditionality: Both units are practitioner judgements of good coping, with no observed damage behind the threat class.

mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__floo.mechanism: Flooding was among the stresses seen at all planted mangrove sites in a national census in Sri Lanka, alongside drought, smothering, strong sun, browsing and trampling by cattle [ev_establishment_survival_kodikara17_3]. In Vietnam's Bac Lieu province mangrove replanting did poorly, mostly because of heavy storms, flooding and poor planting technique [ev_frmg_vnppar_5], and a World Bank coastal planting project in Viet Nam reports that planting at some sites in high flood-risk zones was delayed or failed because of severe weather damage [ev_climate_shock_wbicr6719_2].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__floo.conditionality: None of these accounts separates flood damage from other causes, and the World Bank report does not separate mangrove from other coastal tree planting [ev_establishment_survival_kodikara17_3, ev_frmg_vnppar_5, ev_climate_shock_wbicr6719_2]. Practitioners rate mangrove regeneration in Senegal and planting in Bangladesh as coping well with floods and storm surge, and a Philippine mangrove buffer as coping very well, so the threat reads as slight [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1442_2011_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_4300_2019_storm_surge_coastal_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_578_2016_storm_surge_coastal_flood]. The damage falls on newly planted stands in their first years and depends on where they are planted.

mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__sedi.mechanism: Sediment burial can harm mangroves, but how much depends on how much sediment arrives and how fast. Heavy or sudden burial caused dieback: in Sarawak, Malaysia, the decline of Sonneratia alba in the inner part of a natural stand was attributed to burial of its breathing roots, and no new roots had formed on the dead trees [ev_climate_shock_muro99_1]; on the Mekong coast of Vietnam, forest density fell moving inland as root burial deepened, citing the authors' own earlier measurements [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1]; and large, sudden sedimentation events can bury many trees in a short time and cause large-scale dieback, as also reported, second-hand, along a river in Indonesia loaded with volcanic sediment [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2]. Reviews citing earlier work add that rapid sedimentation can cause delayed death of trees by smothering their aerial roots [ev_establishment_survival_gijsman21_1, ev_climate_shock_ellis04_3]. Mild burial and slow build-up did little harm. In a New Zealand estuary with sedimentation as high as 23 mm a year, mangroves at the muddiest sites were taller, had more breathing roots and new seedlings and were less stressed [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1], though the site with the most sediment showed more deaths of breathing roots and seedlings, which the authors call a potential negative effect [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_2]. In a seedling experiment in China, every species survived a modest burial treatment except the small pioneer Sonneratia apetala, of which 2 of 12 seedlings died [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_2].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__sedi.conditionality: The damage is rated low because only the mild cases give a size: the New Zealand sedimentation rate and the seedling experiment, where harm was small [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1]. The findings of heavy or sudden burial killing trees state no size [ev_climate_shock_muro99_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2], so the low rating should not be read as saying planted mangroves are safe from heavy burial. The field evidence comes from natural or partly natural stands, not from stands stated to be planted; the Vietnam and Indonesia cases are second-hand, and the Sarawak result is a single transect [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2, ev_climate_shock_muro99_1]. The seedling experiment was short and tested only a modest burial dose [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1], and the New Zealand stand is a single-species system in a high-income, temperate setting [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1]. Part of the effect is off-site rather than on the adopting farm.

mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wate.mechanism: In Sri Lanka, mangrove seedlings and propagules planted in the low intertidal zone of the wet zone were exposed to long-term submergence due to heavy rains [ev_establishment_survival_kodikara17_1].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wate.conditionality: This is a single observational source that does not quantify the resulting losses; the exposure is linked to the planting position along the tidal gradient, a siting error rather than a property of the practice.

mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wave.mechanism: Planted mangroves fail where the shore is exposed to waves and erosion. A global review of planted-mangrove survival names wind and wave erosion, along with flooding and drying out, as a common reason restoration projects fail [ev_climate_shock_gorman22_4]. A review of eroding mud coasts, including Indonesia, finds that the loss of sediment behind the erosion also stops mangroves from coming back [ev_climate_shock_winterwerp20_8]. On an eroding shoreline in Singapore, the project team judged simple planting insufficient to rebuild the forest [ev_climate_shock_ellison20_5]. Young seedlings are the weak point. On the Mekong coast of Vietnam, waves and currents eroding the soft muddy bottom of one fringe prevented seedlings establishing, with erosion pins showing 17 cm of erosion there against less than 1 cm on a stable sandy fringe where saplings spread [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_3]; the same paper cites work showing as little as 1–3 cm of vertical erosion can make seedlings fail, and that storm currents dislodge them [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_4]. In a seedling experiment in China, significantly more seedlings died when the bed was eroded than when it was buried, for every species [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_3]. Losses differed by species: all Sonneratia apetala seedlings died [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_6]; Avicennia marina and Laguncularia racemosa each lost 33% dead, with 17% and 42% toppled [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_4, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_5]; Rhizophora stylosa and Kandelia obovata had low survival [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_7, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_8]; and Aegiceras corniculatum seedlings were eroded before growing anchoring roots [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_9]. Bruguiera sexangula survived all erosion treatments, and Bruguiera gymnorhiza fared about as well as Avicennia marina [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_10, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_11].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wave.conditionality: The damage is rated low overall, although several species lost many seedlings in the experiment. No source gives a rate of loss for planted stands: the reviews report other studies' findings [ev_climate_shock_gorman22_4, ev_climate_shock_winterwerp20_8], the Singapore case is the project team's judgement at a single site in a rich country [ev_climate_shock_ellison20_5], the Vietnam erosion contrast covers natural seedlings at two fringes without statistics [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_3], and the 1–3 cm figure is second-hand [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_4]. The seedling losses come from a short tank experiment in which the bed was lowered around seedlings, a stand-in for exposure to waves on an eroding shore, and they vary widely by species [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_3, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_6, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_10]. The risk sits mostly in the first years, while plants are small.

mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wind.mechanism: Strong cyclones can cause moderate damage to mangroves. Reviews report tree damage rising quickly once winds exceed 130 km/h [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_gijsman21_1, ev_establishment_survival_mcivor12_1], and in Florida the 2005 Hurricane Wilma was estimated to have destroyed 1250 ha of mangroves [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_marois15_1]. In the Philippines, after Category 5 Typhoon Odette, 85.71% of trees in planted stands were damaged against 77.14% in natural stands [ev_climate_shock_baring24_1]; Rhizophora stylosa had the most deaths there, 14 of them in planted plots [ev_climate_shock_baring24_2], and a review reports that Rhizophora trees are more likely to die in strong winds because they cannot hold themselves up [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_gijsman21_2]. In Vietnam's Bac Lieu province storms washed out newly planted seedlings before their roots took hold [ev_frmg_vnppar_6, ev_frmg_vnppar_7], and in Bangladesh project staff report cyclones causing severe damage to planted mangroves [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_4]. Authors of a Bangladesh study warn that cyclones can destroy mangroves directly or through raised salinity and lack of oxygen, and that this must be weighed when investing in large replanting programmes [ev_climate_shock_dasgupta19_2]. On St Croix, hurricanes the year after a 1978 restoration planting caused some wash-out and were partly to blame for losses: 40% of 86,000 planted seedlings survived but only 1–2% of the sown propagules [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_1]. After Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines, mangroves older than 32 years had 95% mortality with no recovery, while those younger than 8 years fully recovered within 2 years [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_3]. In Florida and Honduras, hurricane wind and surge killed existing mangrove trees, and the forest floor then sank as the dead roots rotted, so the damage went on after the storm [ev_climate_shock_cah06_1].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wind.conditionality: Practitioners rate mangrove regeneration in Senegal as coping well with local windstorms and planting in Bangladesh as coping moderately with tropical storms [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1442_2011_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_4300_2019_tropical_storm]. The review figures describe existing forest [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_gijsman21_1, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_marois15_1]; the Philippine comparison covers a single bay with few plots after a single extreme storm [ev_climate_shock_baring24_1]; the Vietnam and Bangladesh accounts come from evaluators and project staff, not measurements [ev_frmg_vnppar_6, ev_frmg_vnppar_7, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_4]; and the Bangladesh warning is the authors' general advice [ev_climate_shock_dasgupta19_2]. Planted stands are most at risk before their roots take hold, so the threat to an investment sits in the establishment years. In Japan, a strong typhoon caused no damage to six young planted mangroves, but the authors say this was partly luck: the peak waves came at low tide in a sheltered bay [ev_climate_shock_takagi23_1]. The St Croix and Haiyan results are cited second-hand, and the Haiyan source does not say whether the old and young stands were planted [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_1, ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_3]. The Florida and Honduras finding and the Rhizophora review describe existing forest, and the review cites other studies [ev_climate_shock_cah06_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_gijsman21_2].

mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wind.mechanism: In high-income places the sources agree that cyclones damage mangroves, but none says how much, so the damage is rated low. In Florida, the 2005 Hurricane Wilma was estimated to have destroyed 1250 ha of existing mangroves [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_marois15_1]. In Florida and Honduras, hurricane wind and surge killed existing mangrove trees and the forest floor then sank as the dead roots rotted [ev_climate_shock_cah06_1]. On St Croix, hurricanes the year after a 1978 restoration planting caused some wash-out and were partly to blame for losses, with 40% of 86,000 planted seedlings surviving [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_1].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wind.conditionality: Only the St Croix account concerns planted mangroves, and it is cited second-hand and does not say how much of the loss the hurricanes caused [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_1]. The Florida and Honduras findings describe existing forest, and the Wilma figure is cited in a review [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_marois15_1, ev_climate_shock_cah06_1]. In Japan a strong typhoon caused no damage to six young planted mangroves, but at a single sheltered site where, the authors say, survival was partly luck because the peak waves came at low tide [ev_climate_shock_takagi23_1]. All of this is from rich countries.

mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wind.mechanism: In lower-income settings, project staff on the Bangladesh coast report that cyclones caused severe damage to planted mangroves through species loss and large gaps [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_4], and authors of a Bangladesh study warn that cyclones can destroy mangroves directly or through raised salinity and lack of oxygen, a risk to weigh when investing in large replanting programmes [ev_climate_shock_dasgupta19_2].
mangrove_restoration__asset_threat__wind.conditionality: Practitioners rate mangrove regeneration in Senegal as coping well with local windstorms and mangrove planting in Bangladesh as coping moderately with tropical storms, so the threat reads as slight [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1442_2011_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_4300_2019_tropical_storm]. None of these units is a measurement: the damage report comes from the implementing project's staff and gives no extent [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_4], and the warning is the authors' general advice [ev_climate_shock_dasgupta19_2].

mangrove_restoration__biodiversity_prior.mechanism: In a global meta-analysis of mostly planted mangrove restoration, restored mangroves exhibit higher levels of crab production and diversity than degraded mangroves (RR′ = 0.80, 95% CIs = 0.64 to 0.97) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_su21_1]. A WOCAT mangrove afforestation sheet from Bangladesh reports that the plantation site supports habitats for birds and crabs and develops suitable habitats for wildlife and fish [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4300_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4300_2019_habitat_diversity]. In Vietnam's southern Mekong Delta an independent evaluation relays that forest cover in the protection zones increased from around 50 percent in 2000 to 96 percent in 2007 as a result of the project, and that the zones around mangrove roots protected from the violence of the sea created breeding grounds for fish and shellfish, with sea crabs and shellfish re-appearing in some places and increasing in others [ev_frmg_vnppar_3, ev_frmg_vnppar_4].
mangrove_restoration__biodiversity_prior.conditionality: The same meta-analysis found no major difference in crab or fish production and diversity between restored mangroves and unvegetated tidal flats, and its metric merges production with diversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_su21_2], so the gain depends on the comparison: it holds against degraded mangrove, not against the open tidal flat. The Bangladesh entries are compiler ratings, not measurements. The Vietnam cover figure is before-and-after project data with no counterfactual, which stakeholders described as only partly attributable to the project; it includes casuarina windbreak planting and protection of existing forest, and it is cover rather than a count of species [ev_frmg_vnppar_3]. The return of crabs and shellfish is an anecdotal observation, and it came with protection contracts given to smallholders as well as the replanting [ev_frmg_vnppar_4].

mangrove_restoration__carbon_sequestrati.mechanism: Restored mangroves moderately increase carbon storage. Restored mangroves take up carbon in their trees and store it in waterlogged soils. A global review of measurements found planted mangrove removing up to 23.1 t of CO2 per hectare per year in the first 20 years and 10.5 t in the following 40 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_4], and a global meta-analysis found restored mangroves store more carbon than bare tidal flats [ev_carbon_sequestration_su21_1]. Reforested mangrove is predicted to hold 127.7 Mg C ha−1 in its above-ground trees at 40 years, against 88.7 where mangroves are planted on flats that never had them [ev_carbon_sequestration_song23_1]. Over longer periods, successful rehabilitation can raise soil carbon by 83 to 96 Mg C/ha [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ellison20_4]. Project estimates point the same way: a Viet Nam project reports 1.12 million tons of CO2 equivalent absorbed by 4,028 hectares of regenerated mangrove [ev_carbon_sequestration_gcffp013_2], and a World Bank model for Indonesia gives 38.5 tCO2e per hectare per year for restoring mangrove on old fish ponds [ev_carbon_sequestration_wbidn22_2]. A project in Thailand found higher soil carbon down to two meters in planted areas than in unplanted controls over 18 years, as reported in a review [ev_soil_organic_carbon_prayunita26_1], another review concludes that restoration raises organic carbon in sediments compared with mud flats [ev_soil_organic_carbon_uddin24_1], and a Philippine model estimates that letting 377.25 ha of abandoned fishponds revert to mangrove would add 4691.73 Mg of carbon in vegetation over 6.5 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_duncan16_1].
mangrove_restoration__carbon_sequestrati.conditionality: The gain depends entirely on the plantings surviving, and several sources record failure: in the Philippines about 440 million propagules planted over 20 years averaged only 5 – 10% survival [ev_establishment_survival_winterwerp20_4], an earlier World Bank-funded project had 17-19% survival 10 years after planting [ev_establishment_survival_baring24_3], a Singapore planting lost about 94% of its propagules [ev_establishment_survival_ellison20_1], juvenile mangroves behind sediment dams in Indonesia disappeared after one or two years as the ground sank [ev_establishment_survival_winterwerp20_2], and in Mexico all planting contracts were cancelled for non-compliance [ev_establishment_survival_hernmel17_1]. In Bangladesh, survival of two planted species was less than 50% after five years, and the authors advise planning replacement planting [ev_establishment_survival_dasgupta19_3]; this is the authors' judgement rather than a reported measurement. Other projects report 70–90 percent survival in Viet Nam and averages near 74.3% in Aceh, but these are self-reported by implementers [ev_establishment_survival_wbicr6719_1, ev_establishment_survival_wibsua08_1]. Few units give a size that can be compared, which holds the rating at moderate. The Viet Nam and Indonesia project figures are modelled, the Indonesia total includes avoided pond emissions, and a Senegal model simply assumes a rate for young mangroves [ev_carbon_sequestration_gcffp013_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_wbidn22_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_iisd26_6]. The Thai and review findings are cited second-hand and give no rate, and the Philippine figure is a projection its authors call preliminary [ev_soil_organic_carbon_prayunita26_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_uddin24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_duncan16_1].

mangrove_restoration__carbon_sequestrati.mechanism: In lower-income settings the evidence points both ways. On the benefit side, a Bangladesh project paper reports that new mangrove plantations on newly formed coastal land were designed to absorb carbon each year [ev_carbon_sequestration_ahammad13_3], and a Senegal model assumes young restored mangroves take up 14.6 tonnes of CO2 per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_iisd26_6]. On the harm side, in the Philippines about 440 million mangrove propagules were planted over 20 years, yet survival averaged only 5 – 10% [ev_establishment_survival_winterwerp20_4]. In Bangladesh, the authors of a study of the national planting programme put survival of two planted species at less than 50% after five years and advise planning replacement planting [ev_establishment_survival_dasgupta19_3].
mangrove_restoration__carbon_sequestrati.conditionality: What separates the two sides is whether plantings survive. The benefit side is planned or assumed uptake: the Bangladesh paper is by project staff and gives no measured rate [ev_carbon_sequestration_ahammad13_3], and the Senegal figure is a model input, not a measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_iisd26_6]. The harm side is establishment failure: the Philippine figure is cited second-hand, and the Bangladesh figure is the authors' judgement; both mean little or no carbon was gained from much of what was planted [ev_establishment_survival_winterwerp20_4, ev_establishment_survival_dasgupta19_3]. No source here measures carbon in restored mangroves in a lower-income country, so a project would need its own survival and carbon monitoring before claiming a gain.

mangrove_restoration__carbon_sequestrati.mechanism: The same restoration mechanism (standing mangrove trees and their soils building a carbon store) sits behind both directions pooled here, but this row combines a project where plantings were abandoned with a project where cover grew strongly — so no single mechanism statement can describe the pooled result; the outcome depends entirely on whether restoration was actually sustained.
mangrove_restoration__carbon_sequestrati.conditionality: One side of the evidence: a Mexican restoration programme where, in 2011, all plantation-beneficiary contracts were cancelled for non-compliance, even though natural self-regeneration of white mangrove still recovered 68% of the surface on its own. The other side: a Mekong Delta project where mangrove forest cover serving a coastal-protection function rose from around 50% in 2000 to 96% in 2007. The difference is project delivery and compliance, not the underlying restoration method — a failed, non-compliant planting programme versus a sustained one with strong cover recovery.
mangrove_restoration__carbon_sequestrati.agreement_note: This is why the row is coded as conflicting rather than null: both sides show real, measured effects at opposite ends — plantation failure/cancellation in the Mexican site, versus a near-doubling of forest cover in the Mekong Delta — and the evidence does not let one side dominate the other.

mangrove_restoration__cost_per_hectare_r.mechanism: These are the costs of establishing a hectare of mangrove, mostly by planting. A global database of 249 projects gives a median of $8,143 per hectare, with the middle range of projects between $1,434 and $47,935 [ev_project_cost_goto25_1], an earlier global meta-analysis gives a median of 1,097.16 USD/ha [ev_project_cost_su21_1], and a global cost-carbon study uses an average of US$4368 per hectare [ev_project_cost_jakovac20_3]. Country figures include 427.38 USD/ha (Bangladesh) and 150.00 USD/ha (Philippines) from practitioner records [ev_project_cost_wocat_4300_2019_establishment, ev_project_cost_wocat_578_2016_establishment], US$211/ha for community reforestation in the Philippines and US$946/ha in Thailand [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_4, ev_project_cost_hernmel17_3], 843 US dollars in northern Viet Nam [ev_project_cost_ifrc11_1], about USD 3,550 in Indonesia [ev_project_cost_wbidn22_1], and a modelled 7,700 USD/ha mean for Bangladesh [ev_project_cost_wbmang25_1]. In the Philippines, letting disused fishponds revert to mangrove by breaching the dikes and paying caretakers is costed at USD 1,099.90 per hectare in the first year and about USD 1,097.46 each following year, against USD 2,470.88 per hectare for active planting [ev_project_cost_ferrer11_1, ev_project_cost_ferrer11_2]. A Caribbean study's cost table gives a median of 2,000 per hectare for planting seedlings and saplings outside Florida and the Caribbean (57 studies), against 45,000 in Florida and 23,000 in the Caribbean, in 2019 US$ rounded to the nearest 1,000 [ev_project_cost_beck22_5].
mangrove_restoration__cost_per_hectare_r.conditionality: Costs vary enormously with the site and method, from simple planting of seedlings to rebuilding badly eroded coasts [ev_project_cost_su21_1, ev_project_cost_goto25_1]. Figures use different bases: some state no price year, the global database uses 2022 international dollars [ev_project_cost_goto25_1], the Indonesia figure is a government cost estimate [ev_project_cost_wbidn22_1], the Bangladesh mean is modelled [ev_project_cost_wbmang25_1], and a Mexican figure of US$94.68/ha reflects the budget available rather than the full cost, which the authors judged too low for success [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_1]. For lower-middle-income countries the figures run from about 211 to 7,700 dollars per hectare [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_4, ev_project_cost_wocat_4300_2019_establishment, ev_project_cost_wbmang25_1]. The Philippine fishpond figures are advance estimates from local wage rates and another project's unit costs, not recorded spending [ev_project_cost_ferrer11_1, ev_project_cost_ferrer11_2]. The Caribbean study's medians cover initial direct costs only, pool many countries, and are rounded [ev_project_cost_beck22_5].

mangrove_restoration__cost_per_hectare_r.mechanism: In lower-middle-income settings the costs run from US$211/ha for community-supported mangrove reforestation in the Philippines and a compiler-entered 427.38 USD/ha for mangrove afforestation in Bangladesh, through US$990.96/ha cited for reforestation in Vietnam, to a modelled national mean of 7,700 USD/ha for mangrove restoration in Bangladesh [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_4, ev_project_cost_wocat_4300_2019_establishment, ev_project_cost_hernmel17_5, ev_project_cost_wbmang25_1].
mangrove_restoration__cost_per_hectare_r.conditionality: The Philippine figure excludes preliminary and maintenance activities, which raise it to US$1,156.52/ha [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_5], so figures that omit them understate full cost. The Vietnam value is a citation of the IFRC evaluation with no stated price year, the Bangladesh WOCAT value is a compiler entry converted from local currency, and the 7,700 USD/ha mean is a modelled value transfer from grey literature, far above the observed community-supported planting costs [ev_project_cost_wbmang25_1].

mangrove_restoration__cost_per_hectare_r.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings the reported costs of restoring a hectare of mangrove fall in the moderate range overall but vary widely. At the low end are US$94.68/ha allocated in Tabasco, Mexico [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_1] and a practitioner entry of 150.00 USD/ha for mangrove buffers in the Philippines [ev_project_cost_wocat_578_2016_establishment]. In the middle are 843 US dollars at present value to create one hectare in a community project in northern Viet Nam [ev_project_cost_ifrc11_1] and US$946/ha cited for reforestation in Thailand [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_3]. In the Philippines, turning a disused fishpond back to mangrove was estimated at USD 1,099.90 per ha in the first year by natural regrowth and US$2470.88/ha by active planting [ev_project_cost_ferrer11_1, ev_project_cost_ferrer11_2]. The Indonesian government puts planting at about USD 3,550 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wbidn22_1].
mangrove_restoration__cost_per_hectare_r.conditionality: The lowest value is not a full cost: the Mexican amount was set by the budget available, and the authors argue it was too little for success [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_1]. The Philippine fishpond figures are estimates rather than recorded spending, and the natural-regrowth figure is mostly labour for 5 years of guarding [ev_project_cost_ferrer11_1, ev_project_cost_ferrer11_2]. The Indonesian figure is a government programme cost reported second-hand [ev_project_cost_wbidn22_1]. The Viet Nam figure is a present value from an evaluation commissioned by the implementer, the Thai figure is a citation with no stated price year, and the Philippine buffer figure is a practitioner entry converted from local currency [ev_project_cost_ifrc11_1, ev_project_cost_hernmel17_3, ev_project_cost_wocat_578_2016_establishment].

mangrove_restoration__cost_per_tco2e_avo.mechanism: A global spatial cost-carbon model estimates the break-even carbon price at which carbon payments would cover land opportunity and restoration costs, and finds that carbon prices between 4.5 and 18.0 US$ per tCO2 could support the restoration of 90% of deforested mangroves [ev_project_cost_jakovac20_1].
mangrove_restoration__cost_per_tco2e_avo.conditionality: This is a modelled break-even price from a single global study with no country context, not an observed project cost per tonne; it depends on the assumed opportunity and restoration costs and on the share of carbon credited, and it assumes the restored stands establish.

mangrove_restoration__cost_reduction.mechanism: The only unit is a project cited second-hand from a Tabasco, Mexico, report, where 50 ha of black mangrove were reforested successfully at a full per-hectare cost covering sanitation, dredging, soil conservation works, ridge restoration, staff training, plant production, transplanting and monitoring [ev_project_cost_hernmel17_2].
mangrove_restoration__cost_reduction.conditionality: This is a description of what restoration cost, not a measured saving, so no direction or class is stated for cost reduction. It is a single second-hand project report from an upper-middle-income setting; a second independent source or a measured cost comparison is what is missing, and the source's printed per-hectare value could not be used as a magnitude.

mangrove_restoration__establishment_cost.mechanism: The only figure is a global average restoration cost for mangroves of 2,332 international dollars per hectare per year (2023 prices), compiled in the Ramsar Global Wetland Outlook [ev_project_cost_rgwo25_5].
mangrove_restoration__establishment_cost.conditionality: This is one compiled average with no country or income group, so it cannot set a cost level for lower-income settings [ev_project_cost_rgwo25_5]. It is given per year, unlike the one-off per-hectare costs in the restoration cost evidence, so they should not be compared directly.

mangrove_restoration__flood__all.mechanism: The evidence points to a small reduction in flood impact. Of mangrove restoration projects reviewed worldwide, 50% say the habitat gives better protection from storms [ev_frmg_nara16_5], and a model for northern Vietnam, cited second-hand, finds restoration pays off even more once the saved upkeep of the sea dike behind the mangroves is counted [ev_frmg_erw09_2]. Newer models point the same way: in Bangladesh, mangrove planting belts in front of embankments cut a cyclone surge's water speed by 29–92% but lowered its height only modestly (4–16.5 cm) [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1], and in the Philippines restoring the mangroves lost between 1950 and 2010 would bring more than US $450 million a year in flood protection benefits [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. A global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes finds about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected by flooding each year [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. A Caribbean model of flood protection finds many coastlines where mangroves give long-term flood protection worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per hectare, so that restoration near Port au Prince, Haiti, costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].
mangrove_restoration__flood__all.conditionality: No study here measures a planted stand lowering flood water. The project share is self-reported, and the Vietnam, Bangladesh and Philippine results are all models [ev_frmg_nara16_5, ev_frmg_erw09_2, ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. The Bangladesh and Philippine models treat the restored belts as fully grown forest, so the benefit only arrives once plantings mature, and the Philippine authors warn that much of the lost mangrove land may now be built on [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. The Bangladesh authors add that mangroves alone will not fully protect against large surges and must be combined with embankments [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. The protection falls on the coast, the dikes and the wider public, not as income to the households who plant or tend the mangroves [ev_frmg_erw09_2, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. The global model assumes working dikes behind every restored area and does not include cyclone damage to the mangroves, and its share is small because many coastlines have no mangroves to restore [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. The Caribbean figure is a model of avoided direct damage to property, so it is a break-even value for the public rather than a measured drop in flooding [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].

mangrove_restoration__flood__all__income.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings the evidence points to a moderate reduction in flood impact, all of it from models. In Bangladesh, mangrove planting belts in front of embankments cut a cyclone surge's water speed by 29–92% but lowered its height only modestly (4–16.5 cm) [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. In Haiti, a Caribbean flood-protection model finds restoration near Port au Prince costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back through avoided flood damage [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].
mangrove_restoration__flood__all__income.conditionality: No study here measures a planted stand lowering flood water; both results are models, which is why the rating is held at moderate and confidence is medium. The Bangladesh model treats the planted belts as fully grown forest, so the benefit only comes once plantings mature, and its authors say mangroves alone will not fully protect against large surges and must be combined with embankments [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. The Haiti figure is a break-even value of avoided damage to property, which goes to the public rather than to the households who plant or tend the mangroves [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2]. Neither source covers severe or extreme floods as measured events. Part of the effect is off-site, on the coast and land behind the belt rather than on the adopting farm.

mangrove_restoration__flood__all__income.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings the row holds two units: the compiler for mangrove buffers in the Philippines rates flood impacts as decreased [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_578_2016_flood_impacts], and a second-hand reading of an economic model for coastal districts of northern Vietnam reports that restoration scenarios have even higher cost-benefit ratios when the avoided maintenance cost of the sea dike system, protected from coastal storm surges by the mangroves, is included [ev_frmg_erw09_2].
mangrove_restoration__flood__all__income.conditionality: Neither unit measures flood levels or wave reduction behind a planted stand: the Philippine unit is a compiler rating and the Vietnam unit a model result cited second-hand [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_578_2016_flood_impacts, ev_frmg_erw09_2]. The Vietnam value is the avoided upkeep of a public sea dike, a saving to society rather than income reaching the households working the coast [ev_frmg_erw09_2].

mangrove_restoration__flood_hazard.mechanism: Mangroves in front of sea dykes reduce the damage and upkeep the dykes need: a review cited by an Indian study reports a 20–30% reduction in dyke repair and maintenance costs depending on the width of mangrove in front [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10]. Of mangrove restoration projects reviewed worldwide, 50% report better storm protection [ev_frmg_nara16_5], and a model for northern Vietnam, cited second-hand, finds restoration pays off even more once the saved dike upkeep is counted [ev_frmg_erw09_2]. In Bangladesh, a model of mangrove planting belts finds they cut cyclone surge water speed by 29–92% and surge height by 4–16.5 cm [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1], and in the Philippines a model values restoring mangroves lost between 1950 and 2010 at more than US $450 million a year in flood protection [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. A global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes finds expected flood damage to buildings could fall by US$800 million a year, only 2.3% of damage on mangrove coastlines, with about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. A Caribbean model of flood protection finds many coastlines where mangroves give long-term flood protection worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per hectare, so that restoration near Port au Prince, Haiti, costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].
mangrove_restoration__flood_hazard.conditionality: No study here measures a planted stand lowering flood water. The dyke-cost figure is second-hand and does not say whether the mangroves were planted or existing [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10], the project share is self-reported [ev_frmg_nara16_5], and the other results are models [ev_frmg_erw09_2, ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]; the Bangladesh and Philippine models assume the restored trees are fully grown, so the benefit comes only once plantings mature. The savings fall to the public and to dyke owners, not as income to the households who work the coast. The global model points to a small overall reduction: it assumes working dikes behind every restored area, leaves out cyclone damage to the mangroves, and its share is small because many coastlines have no mangroves to restore [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. The Caribbean figure is a model of avoided direct damage to property, so it is a break-even value for the public rather than a measured drop in flooding [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].

mangrove_restoration__flood_hazard__inco.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings the evidence points to a strong reduction in flood impact, mostly measured in money. A study cited second-hand by an Indian paper reports, for Viet Nam, a 20–30% reduction in sea-dyke repair and maintenance costs depending on the width of mangrove in front of the dyke [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10]. In Haiti, a Caribbean flood-protection model finds restoration near Port au Prince costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back through avoided flood damage [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2]. In Bangladesh, a model of mangrove planting belts finds they cut a cyclone surge's water speed by 29–92% and its height by 4–16.5 cm [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1].
mangrove_restoration__flood_hazard__inco.conditionality: No study here measures a planted stand lowering flood water. The dyke-cost figure is second-hand and does not say whether the mangroves were planted or existing [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10], and the Haiti and Bangladesh results are models [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2, ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. The Bangladesh authors call the drop in surge height modest, assume fully grown trees, and say mangroves must be combined with embankments [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. The savings fall to the public and to dyke owners, not as income to the households who work the coast [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10, ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].

mangrove_restoration__flood_hazard__inco.mechanism: In the Philippines and Viet Nam, mangroves in front of sea dykes cut the cost of protecting the coast. A review cited by an Indian study reports a 20–30% reduction in dyke repair and maintenance costs depending on the width of mangrove in front [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10], a model for northern Vietnam, cited second-hand, finds restoration pays off even more once the saved dike upkeep is counted [ev_frmg_erw09_2], and a Philippine model values restoring mangroves lost between 1950 and 2010 at more than US $450 million a year in flood protection [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2].
mangrove_restoration__flood_hazard__inco.conditionality: All three are models or second-hand figures, not measurements at restored sites [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10, ev_frmg_erw09_2, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. The Philippine model treats restored stands as fully grown forest, and its authors warn that much of the lost mangrove land may now be built on [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. The savings go to the public and to dyke owners, not as income to the households who work the coast.

mangrove_restoration__food_insecurity.mechanism: Restored mangroves give fish, crabs and shellfish places to breed and shelter, which can mean more food from nearby waters. In a rehabilitated mangrove basin in Java, Indonesia, fishing for finfish grew from practically zero to a profitable livelihood within a few years [ev_fish_catch_debrot22_1]. In Aceh, crabs and oysters increased after planting, and women who used to travel up to 3 km for oysters could gather them near the village [ev_fish_catch_wibsua08_3]. In Sri Lankan lagoon villages, more community participation in mangrove restoration was linked to higher fish production per boat [ev_fish_catch_sathi24_2]. A Senegal model assumes restoration raises artisanal fishery output by 3.0%, after a long lag [ev_fish_catch_iisd26_3].
mangrove_restoration__food_insecurity.conditionality: These are catch and harvest gains used as a stand-in for food security; no study measures diets or hunger. The Java fishery has no comparison site, and the authors name other possible causes and a risk of overfishing young fish [ev_fish_catch_debrot22_1]; the Aceh account is anecdotal and written by the implementer [ev_fish_catch_wibsua08_3]; the Sri Lankan link is only weakly significant [ev_fish_catch_sathi24_2]; and the Senegal figure is a model assumption with no source cited [ev_fish_catch_iisd26_3]. Evidence comes from very few sites per country.

mangrove_restoration__gender_inequity.mechanism: In Senegal, large mangrove planting campaigns spread onto mudflats where women traditionally collected shellfish, and women in particular complained about losing these grounds [ev_gender_inequity_cormier16_1].
mangrove_restoration__gender_inequity.conditionality: This is a single study of one country, based on interviews and focus groups; it reports women's complaints, not a measured loss of catch or income [ev_gender_inequity_cormier16_1].

mangrove_restoration__production_gap.mechanism: The evidence points to a small production gain, though the support is weak, mostly in pond farming next to the mangroves. A World Bank project report in Viet Nam cites studies finding that improved mangrove forest more than 5 years old raised aquaculture values by US$359.7/ha and US$276.6/ha, and by US$1,436.8/ha/year in a third study [ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_5, ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_6]. A Senegal model assumes mangrove restoration raises farm productivity by 2.3% [ev_crop_yield_iisd26_5]. Other findings point the other way, for pond farming. In northern Java, Indonesia, the authors judge that mangroves planted on pond walls and inside ponds hamper pond upkeep, and that their leaf litter and shade lower pond yield [ev_aquaculture_yield_bosma20_2]. In the Philippines, a study citing earlier work notes that turning leased brackish fishponds back into mangrove gives up their fish output (these ponds average 1.06 t/ha), although the cited author judges the national loss small and easily replaced [ev_aquaculture_yield_ferrer11_2].
mangrove_restoration__production_gap.conditionality: Both pond findings say mangroves in ponds, or in place of ponds, lower pond yield [ev_aquaculture_yield_bosma20_2, ev_aquaculture_yield_ferrer11_2]. No study here measures pond yield with and without mangroves at a similar level of farming intensity, so the size of that loss is unknown. None of the gains is measured at a project site either: the Viet Nam figures are values borrowed from other studies, and the Senegal figure is a model assumption [ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_6, ev_crop_yield_iisd26_5]. The Indonesian finding is the authors' judgement and the Philippine one is second-hand. What separates the sides is where the mangroves are: beside the ponds in the Viet Nam figures, inside or instead of them in the Indonesian and Philippine findings.

mangrove_restoration__production_gap__in.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings the sources point both ways, so no direction is given. On the gain side, a World Bank project report in Viet Nam cites studies finding that improved mangrove forest more than 5 years old raised aquaculture values by US$359.7/ha and US$276.6/ha, and by US$1,436.8/ha/year in a third study [ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_5, ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_6]. On the loss side, in northern Java, Indonesia, the authors judge that mangroves planted on pond walls and inside ponds hamper pond upkeep, and that their leaf litter and shade lower pond yield [ev_aquaculture_yield_bosma20_2].
mangrove_restoration__production_gap__in.conditionality: What separates the two sides is where the mangroves are: the Viet Nam values concern mangrove forest next to the ponds, while the Indonesian finding concerns mangroves inside the ponds. Neither side is measured at a project site: the Viet Nam figures are borrowed from other studies, and the Indonesian finding is the authors' judgement [ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_6, ev_aquaculture_yield_bosma20_2]. No study here measures pond yield with and without mangroves at a similar level of farming intensity.

mangrove_restoration__recurrent_cost.mechanism: Recurrent costs are compiler-entered annual maintenance costs for mangrove plantations on WOCAT sheets: 241.07 USD per hectare per year for mangrove afforestation in Bangladesh and 20.00 for mangrove buffers in the Philippines [ev_project_cost_wocat_4300_2019_maintenance, ev_project_cost_wocat_578_2016_maintenance].
mangrove_restoration__recurrent_cost.conditionality: Both are WOCAT compiler entries converted from local currency and they differ widely; only the Bangladesh figure falls in the lower-middle-income band used for the class, and neither sheet itemises the maintenance tasks.

mangrove_restoration__rural_poverty.mechanism: Mangrove restoration reaches household incomes mainly through fish, crabs and shellfish. In northern Viet Nam mangroves raised per-hectare yields of shellfish and oysters by 209-789 per cent, adding income for coastal communities [ev_household_income_ifrc11_1]. In a rehabilitated basin in Java a new finfish fishery earns fishers about 1.05 USD per hour [ev_household_income_debrot22_2], and a Philippine survey suggests replanted mangroves add USD 564–2316/ha/y to local incomes [ev_household_income_debrot22_3]. Appraisals of the planting itself are mostly positive: a global meta-analysis finds benefits outweigh costs [ev_economic_return_su21_1], commune benefit-cost ratios in Viet Nam range from 3.06 to 68.92 [ev_economic_return_ifrc11_1], and Mexican pilot sites had positive net present values [ev_frmg_mxicr_1]. A Senegal model assumes women's income from oyster gathering rises by 10% [ev_household_income_iisd26_4]. In Gujarat, India, 34 of 227 households surveyed reported higher fishing income after mangrove planting [ev_household_income_becklange16_1], and in the Philippines a costing of letting disused fishponds revert to mangrove gives benefit-cost ratios of 4.53 to 4.69 [ev_economic_return_ferrer11_1].
mangrove_restoration__rural_poverty.conditionality: No study measures household poverty against a comparison; the outcome is reached through yields, catch and appraisals, most of them projections, grey literature or reports by implementers [ev_economic_return_ifrc11_1, ev_economic_return_wbmang25_1, ev_frmg_erw09_1, ev_frmg_mxicr_1]. One source finds harm: a Bangladesh appraisal projects that most mangrove-and-shrimp systems lose money for landowners in the early years, and two stay below break-even for longer [ev_economic_return_rahman18_4, ev_economic_return_rahman18_5]. Several results are held out because their value goes to society rather than households: a World Bank project in Viet Nam returned only 3.6 percent without counting carbon, giving a negative net value [ev_economic_return_wbicr6719_3]; a Senegal model gives benefit-cost ratios of 2.27 to 5.71 mostly from avoided damage [ev_economic_return_iisd26_7]; and in Indonesia restoration pays in most districts but not where land is valuable, such as Eastern Sumatra and Kalimantan [ev_economic_return_wbidn22_3]. Mangrove planting is also cheaper than breakwaters, but that saving goes to the public [ev_frmg_nara16_3, ev_frmg_nara16_4]. The Gujarat result is household recall with no comparison villages, from grey literature [ev_household_income_becklange16_1], and the Philippine benefits are borrowed from a Thai valuation rather than measured [ev_economic_return_ferrer11_1]. A global model giving benefit-cost ratios between 3 and 6 for restoring mangroves in front of dikes is held out, because its benefit is avoided flood damage to buildings, which goes to society [ev_economic_return_tiggeloven26_2]. A Caribbean model finding that flood-protection benefits outweigh restoration costs along 181 coastal units in 20 countries and territories is held out for the same reason [ev_economic_return_beck22_1].

mangrove_restoration__rural_poverty__inc.mechanism: There is not enough evidence here to say whether mangrove restoration reduces poverty in these settings. Both sources are models of flood protection, not of household income. A Caribbean model finds 181 coastal units across 20 countries and territories where the benefits of mangrove restoration for coastal adaptation outweigh project costs, with Cuba, the Bahamas and the USA holding the most [ev_economic_return_beck22_1]. A global model of restoring mangroves in front of dikes gives a benefit-cost ratio between 3 and 6, depending on the climate and socioeconomic scenario [ev_economic_return_tiggeloven26_2].
mangrove_restoration__rural_poverty__inc.conditionality: Both benefits are avoided flood damage to buildings, which goes to society rather than to the households who plant or work the mangroves, so neither can show an effect on poverty [ev_economic_return_beck22_1, ev_economic_return_tiggeloven26_2]. What is missing is a study of household income or livelihoods from restored mangroves in these settings.

mangrove_restoration__rural_poverty__inc.mechanism: In upper-middle-income countries, mangrove restoration adds to incomes mainly through aquatic harvests. In northern Viet Nam mangroves raised shellfish and oyster yields per hectare by 209-789 per cent [ev_household_income_ifrc11_1], and commune benefit-cost ratios ranged from 3.06 to 68.92 [ev_economic_return_ifrc11_1]. In Java a new finfish fishery in a rehabilitated basin earns fishers about 1.05 USD per hour [ev_household_income_debrot22_2]; in Aceh crabs and oysters increased after planting [ev_fish_catch_wibsua08_3]; in Sri Lankan lagoons more participation in restoration was linked to more fish per boat [ev_fish_catch_sathi24_2]; and Mexican pilot sites had positive net present values [ev_frmg_mxicr_1]. In the Philippines, a costing of letting disused fishponds revert to mangrove gives benefit-cost ratios of 4.53 to 4.69 [ev_economic_return_ferrer11_1].
mangrove_restoration__rural_poverty__inc.conditionality: The evidence shows a direction but no measured size of poverty change: the figures are yields, catches and project appraisals, many self-reported or projected, with no comparison of household poverty [ev_household_income_ifrc11_1, ev_economic_return_ifrc11_2, ev_frmg_erw09_1, ev_frmg_mxicr_1]. Results whose value goes to society are held out: a World Bank project in Viet Nam had a negative net value unless carbon was counted [ev_economic_return_wbicr6719_3], Indonesian restoration loses money where land is valuable [ev_economic_return_wbidn22_3], and the cheaper-than-breakwater and water-service values benefit the public rather than households [ev_frmg_nara16_4, ev_mgM_mxicr_1]. The Philippine benefits are borrowed from a Thai valuation rather than measured [ev_economic_return_ferrer11_1].

mangrove_restoration__soil_erosion_risk.mechanism: Mangroves slow water and trap sediment, so the coast builds up instead of washing away. In Vietnam's southern Mekong Delta, project monitoring reports coastal erosion reduced by 40 percent in Ca Mau because of replanted mangroves [ev_frmg_vnppar_1], and evaluators found mangroves had turned the Soc Trang coast into an area that builds up [ev_frmg_vnppar_2]. In Bangladesh practitioners report less surface runoff under the plantation canopy [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_4300_2019_surface_runoff], and project staff report better land stabilisation [ev_erosion_hazard_ahammad13_2]. In Indonesia, permeable brushwood dams that let mangroves return trapped about 0.5 m of sediment in four months while the coast kept eroding elsewhere [ev_sediment_retention_winterwerp20_1]. In Bangladesh, government mangrove planting on coastal mudflats is reported to have been very effective in building land, with rapid sediment build-up [ev_sediment_retention_becklange16_1]. Detailed observations of a fringe mangrove forest in Vietnam, part of it planted, found the mangroves engineer the landscape, favouring sediment deposition and dissipating waves [ev_sediment_retention_fagh17_5].
mangrove_restoration__soil_erosion_risk.conditionality: Results depend on where and how mangroves are planted. In parts of Bac Lieu the replanted mangroves washed away and the coast kept eroding fast [ev_frmg_vnppar_2], and in Indonesia mangroves planted on pond dykes and inside ponds did not protect the coast: after spring tides and storms the trees stood but most dykes were destroyed [ev_erosion_hazard_bosma20_1]. The Vietnam figures are uncontrolled project monitoring and visual checks [ev_frmg_vnppar_1, ev_frmg_vnppar_2], the Bangladesh evidence is a practitioner rating and a project claim [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_4300_2019_surface_runoff, ev_erosion_hazard_ahammad13_2], and the Indonesian dam results come from authors linked to the implementing organisations [ev_sediment_retention_winterwerp20_1, ev_sediment_retention_winterwerp20_5]. There is no controlled measurement of erosion under mangrove restoration. The Bangladesh account is a summary in grey literature, and much of it is planting on newly formed land rather than restoring lost mangrove [ev_sediment_retention_becklange16_1]. The Vietnam fringe observations describe shoreline building with no size given [ev_sediment_retention_fagh17_5]. Only a few units give a size, which holds the rating at moderate.

mangrove_restoration__soil_erosion_risk_.mechanism: In Bangladesh, government mangrove planting on coastal mudflats is reported to have been very effective in building land, with rapid sediment build-up [ev_sediment_retention_becklange16_1]. Practitioners report less surface runoff under the plantation canopy [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_4300_2019_surface_runoff], and project staff report that afforestation on newly formed land improved land stabilisation [ev_erosion_hazard_ahammad13_2].
mangrove_restoration__soil_erosion_risk_.conditionality: All the evidence comes from Bangladesh and none is a controlled measurement: a grey-literature summary, a practitioner rating and a claim by the implementing project's staff [ev_sediment_retention_becklange16_1, ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_4300_2019_surface_runoff, ev_erosion_hazard_ahammad13_2]. Much of the planting is on newly formed land rather than restoring lost mangrove [ev_sediment_retention_becklange16_1].

mangrove_restoration__soil_erosion_risk_.mechanism: In Vietnam's southern Mekong Delta, project monitoring reports coastal erosion reduced by 40 percent in Ca Mau and the length of building-up coastline increased by 20 percent because of replanted mangroves [ev_frmg_vnppar_1], and evaluators found mangroves had turned the Soc Trang coast into an area that builds up [ev_frmg_vnppar_2]. In Indonesia, permeable brushwood dams that let mangroves return trapped about 0.5 m of sediment in four months while the coast kept eroding elsewhere [ev_sediment_retention_winterwerp20_1], and similar dams in the Mekong Delta also trapped sediment [ev_sediment_retention_winterwerp20_5].
mangrove_restoration__soil_erosion_risk_.conditionality: Only one unit gives a comparable size, which holds the rating at moderate. Planting on pond dykes and inside ponds in Indonesia did not protect the coast [ev_erosion_hazard_bosma20_1], and in parts of Bac Lieu replanted mangroves washed away and erosion continued [ev_frmg_vnppar_2]. The Vietnam results are uncontrolled monitoring and visual checks [ev_frmg_vnppar_1, ev_frmg_vnppar_2], and the dam results come from authors linked to the implementers [ev_sediment_retention_winterwerp20_1, ev_sediment_retention_winterwerp20_5].

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.mechanism: In a national census of mangrove planting sites in Sri Lanka, seedlings planted high in the tidal zone of the dry and arid zones suffered from drought and strong sun [ev_establishment_survival_kodikara17_2]. In northern Australia, a large dieback of existing mangrove forest was linked to prolonged drought and high temperatures [ev_climate_shock_lovelock17_1].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.conditionality: Neither source says how much drought cuts survival. The Sri Lankan finding points to poor siting along the tidal slope as the real cause [ev_establishment_survival_kodikara17_2]. The Australian dieback concerns existing natural forest in a high-income country, is reported second-hand, and coincided with an unusually low sea level as well as heat, so drought alone is not shown to be the cause [ev_climate_shock_lovelock17_1].

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.mechanism: Planted mangroves suffer from flooding in their first years: it was among the stresses at all planted sites in a Sri Lankan census [ev_establishment_survival_kodikara17_3], contributed to poor replanting results in Vietnam's Bac Lieu province [ev_frmg_vnppar_5], and delayed or wrecked planting at some high flood-risk sites in a World Bank project in Viet Nam [ev_climate_shock_wbicr6719_2]. In Florida, a hurricane's storm surge and the water left ponding afterwards killed 10,760 ha of existing mangrove on poorly drained, low-lying inland sites [ev_climate_shock_lagomasino21_2].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.conditionality: The Florida dieback is in existing natural forest in a high-income country and was driven by water trapped behind low ground with no tidal flushing, so it warns against planting on poorly drained sites rather than measuring harm to restored stands [ev_climate_shock_lagomasino21_2]. Another Florida study found a hurricane surge laid down sediment that raised the forest floor rather than damaging it [ev_climate_shock_cah06mg_1]. Practitioners rate mangrove regeneration in Senegal and planting in Bangladesh as coping well with floods, and a Philippine buffer as coping very well [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1442_2011_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_4300_2019_storm_surge_coastal_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_578_2016_storm_surge_coastal_flood]. None of the planted-stand accounts separates flooding from storms and poor planting technique, so the threat reads as slight and sits in the establishment years and in siting [ev_frmg_vnppar_5, ev_climate_shock_wbicr6719_2].

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.mechanism: One monitoring study links a die-back of mangroves to a spell of low sea level. At Mangrove Bay in arid north-western Australia, the forest died back a second time in 2015–2016, when mean sea level fell and soil water salinity was 30% above normal [ev_climate_shock_lovelock17_2].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.conditionality: This is a single site of existing natural forest, not a restoration, in a rich country, and it gives no measure of how much of the forest was lost [ev_climate_shock_lovelock17_2]. There is no evidence here on how often or how badly restored stands are hit by low sea level.

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.mechanism: Reviews say mangroves drown where their soil surface cannot build up as fast as the sea rises. The first states that there are likely threshold rates of sea-level rise beyond which mangrove surfaces can no longer keep up [ev_climate_shock_mcivor13_1]; the other, citing an earlier study, says mangroves are progressively drowned where sediment and root build-up is slower than the local rise in sea level [ev_climate_shock_woodroffe16_2].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.conditionality: Both reviews describe mangroves in general, not restored stands, and neither gives a rate or a size of loss, so the damage is rated low [ev_climate_shock_mcivor13_1, ev_climate_shock_woodroffe16_2]. The first is the authors' judgement and the second is second-hand. This is a long-term threat to a site, over many years, rather than a single event.

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.mechanism: Sediment burial can harm mangroves, but how much depends on how much sediment arrives and how fast. Heavy or sudden burial caused dieback: in Sarawak, Malaysia, the decline of Sonneratia alba in the inner part of a natural stand was attributed to burial of its breathing roots, and no new roots had formed on the dead trees [ev_climate_shock_muro99_1]; on the Mekong coast of Vietnam, forest density fell moving inland as root burial deepened, citing the authors' own earlier measurements [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1]; and large, sudden sedimentation events can bury many trees in a short time and cause large-scale dieback, as also reported, second-hand, along a river in Indonesia loaded with volcanic sediment [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2]. Reviews citing earlier work add that rapid sedimentation can cause delayed death of trees by smothering their aerial roots [ev_establishment_survival_gijsman21_1, ev_climate_shock_ellis04_3], and that the effect depends on the sediment's texture and on how much arrives and how fast [ev_climate_shock_woodroffe16_1]. In Florida after Hurricane Irma, trees under a thicker layer of storm-deposited mud were more likely to die in the following months, though the mud did not affect how many died at first [ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_3]. Mild burial and slow build-up did little harm. In a New Zealand estuary with sedimentation as high as 23 mm a year, mangroves at the muddiest sites were taller, had more breathing roots and new seedlings and were less stressed [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1], though the site with the most sediment showed more deaths of breathing roots and seedlings, which the authors call a potential negative effect [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_2]. In a seedling experiment in China, every species survived a modest burial treatment except the small pioneer Sonneratia apetala, of which 2 of 12 seedlings died [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_2].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.conditionality: The damage is rated low because only the mild cases give a size: the New Zealand sedimentation rate and the seedling experiment, where harm was small [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1]. The findings of heavy or sudden burial killing trees state no size [ev_climate_shock_muro99_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2], so the low rating should not be read as saying planted mangroves are safe from heavy burial. The field evidence comes from natural or partly natural stands, not from stands stated to be planted; the Vietnam and Indonesia cases are second-hand, and the Sarawak result is a single transect [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2, ev_climate_shock_muro99_1]. The seedling experiment was short and tested only a modest burial dose [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1], and the New Zealand stand is a single-species system in a high-income, temperate setting [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1]. The Florida result is from a single hurricane in a high-income setting and gives no size either [ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_3]. Part of the effect is off-site rather than on the adopting farm.

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.mechanism: Cyclones can cause moderate damage to mangrove stands. After Category 5 Typhoon Odette in the Philippines, 85.71% of trees in planted stands were damaged against 77.14% in natural stands [ev_climate_shock_baring24_1], and most of the Rhizophora stylosa deaths, 14 trees, were in planted plots [ev_climate_shock_baring24_2]. Red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) was significantly less resistant to hurricane damage than black mangrove (Avicennia germinans) in the French Caribbean [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_3], and a review reports higher death rates for Rhizophora trees in strong winds [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_gijsman21_2]. In the French Caribbean, Hurricane Hugo stripped 19% to 71% of the trunk area from the worst-hit stands [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_1], and recovery took about as long as the usual gap between hurricanes, so stands may never fully recover [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_2]. In Florida, 62% of mangroves suffered canopy damage from Hurricane Irma, worst in tall forests [ev_climate_shock_lagomasino21_1], and in Australia Cyclone Debbie damaged 18.1% of mangrove trees in the affected area [ev_climate_shock_rowl26mg_1]. Newly planted stands in Vietnam and Bangladesh were also lost or badly damaged by storms before they established [ev_frmg_vnppar_6, ev_frmg_vnppar_7, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_4]. In Australia, Category 5 Cyclone Yasi caused severe windthrow on 16% of 13,795 ha of mangroves, worst in Rhizophora stands as winds passed 280 km/hr [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_1], and many damaged areas showed no or very limited recovery, with canopy cover falling from above 90% to below 20% [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_2]. In the Florida Keys, tree mortality after Hurricane Irma rose to 36.6% after 9 months, and to 19.8% at a less hard-hit site [ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_1, ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_2]. A review puts full recovery of a hurricane-damaged forest at 20–30 years, given enough time between hurricanes [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_2]. For planted stands, hurricanes on St Croix were partly to blame for losses the year after a restoration planting [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_1], and after Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines mangroves younger than 8 years fully recovered within 2 years while those older than 32 years had 95% mortality [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_3]. In Florida and Honduras, trees killed by hurricane wind and surge left the forest floor sinking as the dead roots rotted [ev_climate_shock_cah06_1].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__ass.conditionality: Most of the measured damage is in existing natural forest in high-income places (Florida, Australia, the French Caribbean), so it informs the risk to restored stands only indirectly [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_1, ev_climate_shock_lagomasino21_1, ev_climate_shock_rowl26mg_1, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_marois15_1]. The planted-stand evidence is a single Philippine bay with few plots [ev_climate_shock_baring24_1], plus reports from evaluators and project staff in Vietnam and Bangladesh [ev_frmg_vnppar_6, ev_frmg_vnppar_7, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_4], and practitioner ratings from Senegal and Bangladesh judge their stands as coping well or moderately [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1442_2011_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_4300_2019_tropical_storm]. Taller stands tend to suffer more [ev_climate_shock_lagomasino21_1]. The risk is sharpest in the establishment years and where hurricanes return often [ev_climate_shock_dasgupta19_2, ev_climate_shock_imbert18_2]. The Yasi, Irma and recovery-time results are also existing forest in high-income countries [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_1, ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_1, ev_climate_shock_krauss23_2]. In Japan a strong typhoon caused no damage to six young planted mangroves, but at a single sheltered site where, the authors say, survival was partly luck [ev_climate_shock_takagi23_1]. The St Croix and Haiyan results are cited second-hand [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_1, ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_3]. The species comparison and the forest-floor finding are also from existing forest in rich countries, and the Rhizophora review cites other studies [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_3, ev_climate_shock_cah06_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_gijsman21_2].

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__car.mechanism: Mangroves moderately increase carbon storage. Mangroves take up carbon in trees and bury it in waterlogged soils, where it can stay for very long periods [ev_mg_carbon_sp14_20261030]. A global review of measurements found planted mangrove removing up to 23.1 t of CO2 per hectare per year in the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_2], a meta-analysis found restored mangroves store more carbon than bare tidal flats [ev_carbon_sequestration_su21_1], and reforested mangrove is predicted to hold 127.7 Mg C ha−1 above ground at 40 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_song23_1]. Successful rehabilitation can raise soil carbon by 83 to 96 Mg C/ha over longer periods [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ellison20_4], and existing mangrove soils that build up as sea level rises keep adding about 1.3–2.0 Mg C per hectare each year [ev_carbon_sequestration_sanderman18_4]. Clearing mangroves releases this store: converting mangrove to shrimp ponds lost 90% of soil carbon in the top 3 m in one study [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sanderman18_2], and 54% of below-ground carbon on average after conversion to ponds and pasture in another [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sanderman18_3]. A project in Thailand found higher soil carbon down to two meters in planted areas than in unplanted controls over 18 years, as reported in a review [ev_soil_organic_carbon_prayunita26_1], another review concludes that restoration raises organic carbon in sediments compared with mud flats [ev_soil_organic_carbon_uddin24_1], and a Philippine model estimates that letting 377.25 ha of abandoned fishponds revert to mangrove would add 4691.73 Mg of carbon in vegetation over 6.5 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_duncan16_1].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__car.conditionality: The clearance figures describe what is lost from existing forest, which shows why restoring cleared land matters but is not a measure of what restoration adds [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sanderman18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_sanderman18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_sanderman18_3]. The restoration gain depends on survival, and several sources record failure, including average survival of only 5 – 10% for about 440 million propagules planted in the Philippines [ev_establishment_survival_winterwerp20_4], about 94% propagule loss in Singapore [ev_establishment_survival_ellison20_1] and planting contracts cancelled in Mexico [ev_establishment_survival_hernmel17_1]. In Bangladesh, survival of two planted species was less than 50% after five years, and the authors advise planning replacement planting [ev_establishment_survival_dasgupta19_3]; this is the authors' judgement rather than a reported measurement. Survival reports of 70–90 percent from Viet Nam and similar figures from Aceh are self-reported by implementers [ev_establishment_survival_wbicr6719_1, ev_establishment_survival_wibsua08_1]. Few units give a comparable size, which holds the rating at moderate, and the project totals from Viet Nam and Indonesia are modelled [ev_carbon_sequestration_gcffp013_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_wbidn22_2]. The Thai and review findings are cited second-hand and give no rate, and the Philippine figure is a projection its authors call preliminary [ev_soil_organic_carbon_prayunita26_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_uddin24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_duncan16_1].

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__flo.mechanism: Mangrove belts strongly reduce flood impacts on the land behind them. Mangrove belts slow and break waves and, far more weakly, lower storm-surge water as it passes through the forest [ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_1, ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_3]. A meta-analysis of field measurements finds existing mangroves cut wave heights by 31% [ev_frmg_nara16_1], and measured surge peaks fall by 5 to 50 centimetres per kilometre of mangrove width [ev_flood_hazard_mcivor12_1, ev_flood_hazard_krauss09_1]. A global model estimates 28% more people would be flooded each year if current mangroves were lost [ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1], and a Philippine model gives 24% more [ev_flood_hazard_wbphl17_1]. After super cyclones in India and Bangladesh, villages sheltered by the existing mangrove forest had less salt water in houses and crop fields, and in Bangladesh flood water stood in crop fields for fewer days, than villages without mangroves [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7]. A World Bank model for Bangladesh finds mangrove belts protect embankments from erosion and strong currents [ev_erosion_hazard_wbmang25_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wbmang25_2, ev_flood_hazard_wbmang25_2], and a second Bangladesh model finds planted belts cut surge water speed sharply but surge height only modestly [ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1]. Of restoration projects reviewed, 50% report better storm protection [ev_frmg_nara16_5], and a Philippine model values restoring mangroves lost since 1950 at more than US $450 million a year in avoided flood damage [ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. In New Zealand, an existing mangrove forest about 1 km wide with no drainage channels lowered peak water by about 24 cm per km [ev_flood_hazard_montgomery18_1], and a global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes finds about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected by flooding each year [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. A Caribbean model of flood protection finds many coastlines where mangroves give long-term flood protection worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per hectare, so that restoration near Port au Prince, Haiti, costing less than $168,000 per hectare would still pay back [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__flo.conditionality: Almost all the sized evidence describes existing mangrove forest, not planted stands: the wave meta-analysis, the Florida surge measurements, the global and Philippine models and the Indian and Bangladesh village comparisons all compare having standing mangroves with losing them [ev_frmg_nara16_1, ev_flood_hazard_krauss09_1, ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1, ev_flood_hazard_wbphl17_1, ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7]. That a planted belt will do the same is assumed, not measured. Lowering of surge and tidal water is much weaker than wave reduction [ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_3, ev_flood_hazard_mcivor12_2], and the World Bank Bangladesh model finds mangroves change total design water level by less than 4% because the surge dominates [ev_flood_hazard_wbmang25_1]. The village studies are small surveys after a single cyclone that their authors call only indicative [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7]. The restoration-specific evidence is weak: the project share is self-reported, and the Vietnam, Bangladesh and Philippine restoration results are models that assume mature trees [ev_frmg_nara16_5, ev_frmg_erw09_2, ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. Benefits fall on the coast and the public at large, partly away from the farm. A no-effect result lowers the rating: in a similar New Zealand forest cut by drainage channels there was no measurable drop in water level, because the water ran along the channels [ev_flood_hazard_montgomery18_2]; this matters for planting on low, channelled mudflats. The global restoration model assumes working dikes behind every restored area and leaves out cyclone damage to the mangroves [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1]. The Caribbean figure is a model of avoided direct damage to property, so it is a break-even value for the public rather than a measured drop in flooding [ev_avoided_damage_value_beck22_2].

mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__flo.mechanism: For cropland behind the coast the most direct evidence is two village surveys after super cyclones. In Bhitarkanika, India, the village with neither mangroves nor an embankment had the most salt water in its crop fields and the village sheltered by the mangrove forest the least [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7]; in the Sundarbans of Bangladesh, households sheltered by the forest recalled flood water standing in their crop fields for about 5 days against about 8 days elsewhere [ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7]. Behind this sits the general coastal-protection evidence: existing mangroves cut wave heights by 31% in a meta-analysis of field measurements [ev_frmg_nara16_1], surge peaks fall by 5 to 50 centimetres per kilometre of mangrove [ev_flood_hazard_mcivor12_1], and a global model estimates 28% more people would be flooded each year if current mangroves were lost [ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1]. Of restoration projects reviewed, 50% report better storm protection [ev_frmg_nara16_5]. In New Zealand, an existing mangrove forest about 1 km wide with no drainage channels lowered peak water by about 24 cm per km [ev_flood_hazard_montgomery18_1], and a global model of restoring all restorable mangroves in front of dikes finds about 140,000 fewer people (3%) affected by flooding each year [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1].
mangrove_restoration__tidal_coastal__flo.conditionality: Both village surveys compare places beside an existing forest with places without one; no planting was involved, the results rest on few sites and household recall, and the authors call them only indicative [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7]. Most other sized evidence also describes existing mangroves, and the restoration-specific results are self-reported or modelled with mature trees assumed [ev_frmg_nara16_1, ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1, ev_frmg_nara16_5, ev_flood_hazard_dasgupta19_1, ev_avoided_damage_value_wbphl17_2]. Surge and tidal water is lowered much less than waves [ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_3], and a World Bank Bangladesh model finds mangroves change total design water level by less than 4% [ev_flood_hazard_wbmang25_1]. No unit measures a cropping outcome beyond the two field-flooding comparisons, so this row takes its rating from the all-systems coastal evidence. A no-effect result lowers the rating: in a similar New Zealand forest cut by drainage channels there was no measurable drop in water level, because the water ran along the channels [ev_flood_hazard_montgomery18_2]; this matters for planting on low, channelled mudflats. The global restoration model assumes working dikes behind every restored area and leaves out cyclone damage to the mangroves [ev_flood_hazard_tiggeloven26_1].
